title: Durability of Running Economy: Differences between Quantification Methods and Performance Status in Male Runners
authors: Zanini M, Folland JP, Blagrove RC
population: Well-trained male runners (VO2max 62.4 mL/kg/min; 10 km 35:50 +/- 4:40); subgroups of high (10 km 31:20) and low (10 km 41:50) performers
findings: During a 90-min run at LT1, RE deterioration was only fractionally larger as oxygen cost than energy cost (0.1% greater from 30-90 min, P<0.001).
After 90 min, RE worsened less in the high-performance group than the low-performance group: energy cost +2.3% vs +4.3% (P<0.01) and oxygen cost +2.4% vs +4.5% (P<0.01).
At standardised distances the difference held, for example at 16.7 km: +1.0 vs +3.2% energy cost (P<0.01).
Authors conclude RE deterioration depends on performance level, with high performers showing superior RE durability.
limitations: Male runners only; laboratory 90-min run at LT1; subgroup comparison, not randomised; RE only, not threshold or HR.
implications: Expect faster (better-trained) runners to decay less in economy over 90 min; use performance level as a covariate in any durability prior, with the default decay larger for slower or less-trained runners.
Use a standardised duration or distance when comparing durability across runs, because magnitudes differ by time versus distance reference.
